newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: France raps U.S. on world trade, U.N., Iraq.
newsitem.headline: France raps U.S. on world trade, U.N., Iraq.

text.p: France told the United States on Wednesday to stop trying to regulate world trade despite allied protests and divorced itself from U.S. efforts to dump U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.

Foreign Minister Herve de Charette also told reporters he had written to Boutros-Ghali saying the so-called oil-for-food deal with Iraq should be implemented immediately because the recent crisis appeared to have subsided.

In his speech to the U.N. General Assembly, he said: "France and Europe do not accept that one country, even if it is the most powerful, is trying to regulate world trade by itself by means of decisions that have extraterritorial scope.
"The World Trade Organisation does not allow it, and no one should doubt the firmness of French and European reactions were such measures actually to be implemented."
He told reporters earlier that U.S. actions on trade had "shocked" nations not only in Europe but in the Middle East and Asia as well.

The United States stepped up its 35-year-old embargo of Cuba in March with the Helms-Burton act, which seeks to isolate the Communist-ruled island by curbing foreign investment. Other nations are also protesting trade curbs against Libya and Iran for alleged involvement in terrorism.
"Unilateralism -- behind this technocratic word there lurks the temptation to impose the law of the strongest at the expense of dialogue and negotiation," de Charette said.

Asked by reporters how Paris would deal with the Clinton administration's decision to use its veto in the Security Council to deny Boutros-Ghali a second term, he reaffirmed France's support for the veteran Egyptian diplomat but suggested it would support another candidate from Africa if it were impossible to get Boutros-Ghali re-elected.
"The French position is fairly straightforward," he said. "It is customary for a secretary-general to serve two terms. An African should serve as secretary-general."
He added, "Those who are seeking to dump him have no clear idea who will succeed him."

He also also took issue with U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright's stated belief that the next secretary-general should primarily be an administrator and concentrate on restructuring the bureaucracy of the world body. He said a secretary-general had to fulfil a variety of tasks and "therefore we expect from him a vision of the world" as well as managerial skills.

On Iraq, de Charette said he wrote to Boutros-Ghali saying that it should now be possible to implement a Security Council offer allowing Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil to buy food and medicine after six years of U.N. trade sanctions.

"We feel today that the climate has eased somewhat and the temperature has dropped," he said in reference to Iraq's offensive into Kurdish areas and the missiles the United States launched in response. "We have a responsiblity to do something about the tragic fate of the Iraqi population."

He said no Security Council resolution authorised the new U.S. extension of the southern no-fly zone over Iraq, although he acknowledged that the original flight bans, which France supported, were also outside the sphere of the United Nations.

He said that after the Gulf War, it was necessary to stop Iraq's "mistreatment" of the Kurds in the north and the Shi'ite Moslems in the South. But the new action challenged the Baghdad government's authority over its territory, and this ran counter to U.N. resolutions, he said.
